entries.text: A Hudson’s Bay Company party under Alexander McLeod meets the coastal communities of the central and southern Oregon coast. The creator calls this “the first known local contact with white people, horses, cloth, metal tools, and guns.”
entries.source: Zybach to the Oregon Travel Information Council, 27 July 2023, p. 4

entries.text: Smith’s journal of the first expedition to California opens “at our rendezvous at a place known as the bend of Bear River,” where he and his partners Jackson and Sublette agreed to divide the company.
entries.source: Jedediah Smith’s journal, 7 August 1826 – 3 July 1827, p. 1

entries.text: Harrison G. Rogers begins his first journal with the inventory of merchandise “taken by Jedediah S. Smith for the Southwest expedition.”
entries.source: Journal of Harrison G. Rogers, 15 August 1826, p. 1

entries.text: Smith writes to William Clark, Superintendent of Indian Affairs at St Louis. The letter is entered in the superintendent’s letterbook and reprinted in the Missouri Republican that October.
entries.source: Jedediah Smith to William Clark, 12 July 1827

entries.text: “My preparations being made I left the Depo on the 13th July 1827 with eighteen men and such supplies as I needed.” The second expedition to California begins.
entries.source: Jedediah Smith’s journal, second expedition, p. 1

entries.text: The party’s camp is recorded at Hogback Ridge.
Rogers opens his second journal with the roll of the men travelling with Smith, and the day’s march: “several very steep, rocky and brushy points of mountains to go up and down.”
entries.source: The second journal of Harrison G. Rogers, 10 May 1828, p. 1

entries.text: The party’s camp is recorded at Gans Prairie.
The party’s camp is recorded at Blue Creek Mountain.
The party’s camp is recorded at the Winchuck River.
The party’s camp is recorded at the Rogue River.
The party’s camp is recorded at the Coquille River.
The party’s camp is recorded at Sunset Bay.

Rogers: “We crossed in Ind. canoes; a great many Inds. live along the river bank; there houses built after the fashion of a shed. A great many Inds. in camp with fish and berris for sale; the men bought them as fast as they brought them.” The creator chose this passage for the top of the proposed interpretive sign.
entries.source: Rogers, 9 July 1828, as quoted in the sign draft of 26 July 2023, p. 1

entries.text: The party’s camp is recorded at Umpqua Bay.
The last entry in Rogers’s journal. The creator’s guidebook heads the day “Defeat River.”

The attack. The creator’s guidebooks describe “the site near the confluence of the Smith and Umpqua Rivers where fourteen of Smith’s men were surprised and killed by Kelawatsets while in camp, preparing to continue their journey to Fort Vancouver,” and add: “You may be surprised to learn that early accounts of the attack may not tell the whole story.” His project index gives the number as fifteen; his second field report calls it “the 14 or 15 beaver trappers killed near here.”
entries.source: Guidebook #2, p. 3; ORWW 1828 Umpqua Memorial Project index

entries.text: Arthur Black reaches Fort Vancouver at ten at night, “in his opinion at the time, the only survivor.”
entries.source: John McLoughlin, 10 August 1828, as quoted in the sign draft of 26 July 2023, p. 1

entries.text: McLoughlin writes to the Honourable Committee of the Hudson’s Bay Company that Smith’s men have been “massacred by the Natives of the Um[p]qua River.”
entries.source: John McLoughlin to the Honourable Committee, 10 August 1828

entries.text: McLoughlin sends Michel La Framboise, Thomas McKay and six other servants to the Umpqua to search for survivors and recover the property.
Alexander Roderick McLeod’s journal of the recovery expedition opens.
entries.source: Journal of Alexander Roderick McLeod, 6 September – 10 December 1828

entries.text: The party’s camp is recorded at Fort Umpqua.

McLeod: “Stoped at the entrance of the North Branch, where Mr. Smiths Party were destroyed, and a Sad Spectacle of Indian barbarity presented itself to our View, the Skeletons of eleven of those Miserabl Sufferers lying bleaching in the Sun, after paying the last Service to their remains we continued forward and made the Coast, no Indians in the Vicinity, contrary to their former Custom as several Villages used to be about this place, the Natives are now more Collected than formerly.” Eleven of the dead were buried that day. The creator’s guidebook heads the entry “Umpqua Burials.”
entries.source: McLeod, 28 October 1828, as printed in the sign draft of 20 October 2023, p. 6; Guidebook #3, contents, p. 17

entries.text: George Simpson writes to Smith from Fort Vancouver. The letter opens the fourth guidebook.
Smith, Jackson & Sublette report to the Secretary of War. The creator’s guidebook dates the letter to Eaton 30 October 1830; the file of the letter itself is dated 29 October.
entries.source: Guidebook #4, contents, p. 9; Smith, Jackson & Sublette to the Secretary of War

entries.text: Bob Zybach submits “A. Black, Jedediah Smith, and the Location of the Hudson’s Bay Company Pack Trails in Northwest Oregon in 1828” to the Department of English at Oregon State University.
entries.source: Zybach, pack trails draft, title page

entries.text: “The 1828 Umpqua Memorial Project had its official beginning on July 20, 2000 with a front page headline article in The Reedsport Courier about a series of local events centered on the history of Jedediah Smith.” The article quotes Wayne Knauf, James C. Auld, Al LePage, Portia Harris and Tom Hedgepeth. “A prayer and wreath was cast in the water while the names of the slain trappers were read.”

“The following year Knauf was joined in his research by good friend and business associate, Don Whereat, another Smith enthusiast and Quuiich Tribal Historian. Whereat was local and field mapped the July 13 and 14 routes most likely taken by Smith and his men.”
Zybach presents the coming Rendezvous to the Northwest Chapter of the Oregon-California Trails Association.
Five indexed GIS map sheets are completed for the guidebooks by Vyla Grindberg of Douglas County GIS.
entries.source: ORWW 1828 Umpqua Memorial Project index; Maps folder

entries.text: The four Rendezvous guidebooks are dated.
The Oregon Commission on Historic Cemeteries confirms in writing that “the Smith Jackson & Sublette Burial Site in Douglas County is listed with the Oregon Commission on Historic Cemeteries.”
entries.source: Kuri Gill, Historic Cemeteries Program Coordinator, to Bob Zybach, 29 March 2023

entries.text: The Jedediah Smith Society 2023 Rendezvous begins at Crescent City. It runs four days, to Fort Vancouver.
On the second day the party visits the ground at the mouth of the Smith River. “Consensus discussion was that a monument or marker should be established to honor the dead buried there.”
At Champoeg on the third day, ORWW director David Gould offers to donate a large stone for the memorial.
Zybach reports on the Rendezvous to the Northwest Chapter of the Oregon-California Trails Association in a forty-seven-slide presentation.

A canine search is made for the trappers’ graves, with Max, a trained cadaver dog handled by Cathy Schneider of Northwest Canine Resources. Six photographs are filed. The Library registers the search and does not publish its findings or its ground.
Cathy Schneider files a report and a field map on the search. Both are described here and neither is reproduced.
Zybach’s account of the Rendezvous appears as the lead article of Castor Canadensis, the Journal of the Jedediah Smith Society, vol. 2 no. 1.
Zybach, David Gould and Dale Hanson choose the memorial stone at the Main Rock quarry at North Bend and settle on an inset bronze plaque.

The stone is loaded at the quarry by Main Rock, hauled by Coos Bay Timber Operators and set by Mast Brothers. “The Memorial stone and all related time, equipment, and services have been entirely donated to this point by these three local businesses.”

Zybach speaks to the Culture Committee of the Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians and writes the same evening summarising the four parts of the project, inviting the Tribes to co-sponsor the memorial stone and saying: “The more Tribal involvement in these observations, the better.”
entries.source: Zybach to Patricia Whereat Phillips, 20 July 2023, p. 1

entries.text: The Umpqua Memorial Committee asks the Oregon Travel Information Council to replace the Bolon Island highway panel with one “more accurate historically and relevant locally.”
entries.source: Zybach to Beth Dehn, Oregon Travel Information Council, 27 July 2023, p. 1

entries.text: The Oregon Travel Information Council’s historical marker committee papers are dated. Thirty-three pages; a third-party document, identified by reference.
Larry Hager of Bronzecraft Memorials at Wamic holds the finished bronze plaque. The mould is poured at 2,300 to 2,400 degrees.
Stu Richardson of Richardson Masonry, Reedsport, cuts the stone to take the plaque and installs it.
Lori Tobias reports on the project for OregonLive; the piece runs in The Oregonian the next day.

The memorial stone is dedicated at sunset, on the 195th anniversary of the burial. The names of the men killed on 14 July 1828 are read and a moment of silence kept. “Sunset was just a few minutes after the rising of full moon on this date.”
David Rupkalvis reports the dedication on the front page of The World at Coos Bay.
The third photographic report is published. Its last page announces a fourth, on the construction and installation of the memorial sign kiosk. No fourth report is in the creator’s published folder.
The last of the interpretive-sign design files is posted. The sign itself is not recorded as installed in the creator’s published folder.
entries.source: Historical Markers, Smith River, Sign, Design folder — file dates
